overview: The Republic of Moldova declared independence in 1991 and adopted its constitution in 1994. This is the modern state, not the medieval principality of Moldavia. The outline includes territory beyond the central government’s effective control in Transnistria, so it must not be read as a map of uniform political control.

periods.title: The independent republic
periods.summary: The map begins in the year of the republic’s 1994 constitution.

sections.title: A woven wall could tell a family story

items.text: Wall carpets in Moldova and neighbouring Romania traditionally helped insulate and decorate houses. Patterns could identify a weaver’s community. Their makers combined practical household use with complex colour and design, turning a warm wall covering into something worth displaying.

Carpets also formed part of brides’ dowries and accompanied important family ceremonies. In funeral customs they could symbolise passage to the afterlife. These are documented cultural meanings attached to textiles, rather than properties of the wool itself.

Weavers work on vertical or horizontal looms, building the design through repeated thread work. Skills have passed through families and also through classes, workshops and museums. The craft links patient hand movements with memories of particular people and places.

Mărțișor customs celebrate the beginning of spring with red-and-white threads that people make, give and wear. The shared regional tradition includes untying the thread when a flowering tree, swallow or stork signals spring’s arrival. Weather watching becomes part of a personal ornament.

Older women, teachers, craftspeople and museum workshops teach thread-making skills. UNESCO records the practice in Moldova, Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia. People attach protective meanings to the colours and objects, while children learn a small craft that can be given to someone else.

A school assessment conducted in 2023 and 2024 covered 968 institutions in Moldova. At that time, pupils in 88 schools had access only to outdoor toilets. This is a concrete reminder that school life includes warmth, privacy and a place to wash hands as well as textbooks.

At Baimaclia’s Mihai Eminescu Gymnasium, staff described the difficulty of children going outside to use toilets in cold weather. Hard water affected pipes and fixtures, and there was no central sewerage connection. Improving a bathroom could therefore involve both plumbing and wider village infrastructure.

A 2026 workshop taught school staff how to inspect and maintain sanitation facilities, spot faults and keep supplies available. A new tap is useful only while water comes out of it. The programme treated everyday cleaning and repairs as part of protecting children’s learning environment.

In August 2020, national ministries and international partners produced Romanian-language handbooks for pupils returning to education during COVID-19. The guides addressed the journey to school, classrooms, libraries, canteens and toilets. They also included advice about emotional well-being.

A My Schedule section helped students record opening times, lesson starts, canteen access and digital learning tools. Separate materials served primary, secondary and vocational education. These surviving guides show how an international emergency rearranged the ordinary timetable of a child’s day.

sections.title: Writing and living with political change

items.text: The 1991 independence declaration describes Moldova as “SUVERAN, INDEPENDENT ŞI DEMOCRATIC”, meaning “sovereign, independent and democratic”. This Romanian wording appears in the Constitutional Court’s 2022 printed edition, page 11. It is a documented modern text using Latin letters, not a medieval inscription.

Armed conflict in 1992 divided control around the Dniester, also called the Nistru. Later negotiations included practical confidence-building between the sides. The OSCE’s 2014 account emphasised solutions that could improve daily contacts while the larger political dispute remained unresolved.

ending.text: The modern republic continues; the unresolved Transnistrian conflict complicates effective control within its internationally recognised borders.
